title: Master Cherry gives the piece of wood to his friend Geppetto, who takes it to make himself a wonderful puppet that can dance, fence with a sword, and turn somersaults.
paragraphs: Just then there was a knock at the door.
“Come in,” said the carpenter, without the strength to stand up.

Then a lively little old man called Geppetto came into the workshop; but whenever the children nearby wanted to make him furious, they called him Polendina, or Little Corn Porridge, because of his yellow wig, which looked very much like corn porridge.
Geppetto had a terrible temper. Just try calling him Polendina! He would turn into a wild beast at once, and there was no holding him back.
“Good morning, Master Antonio,” said Geppetto. “What are you doing down there on the floor?”
“Teaching the ants to count.”
“I hope it does you some good.”
“What brought you here, my friend Geppetto?”
“My legs. You see, Master Antonio, I’ve come to ask you a favour.”
“Here I am, ready to help,” replied the carpenter, rising onto his knees.
“This morning an idea dropped into my head.”
“Let’s hear it.”

“I thought I’d make myself a fine wooden puppet: but a wonderful puppet that can dance, fence with a sword, and turn somersaults. With this puppet I want to travel the world, to earn myself a crust of bread and a glass of wine: what do you think?”
“Bravo, Polendina!” cried the same tiny voice, whose hiding place nobody could work out.
Hearing himself called Polendina, Geppetto turned as red as a pepper with anger, and turning towards the carpenter, he said furiously:
“Why are you insulting me?”
“Who’s insulting you?”
“You called me Polendina!”
“It wasn’t me.”
“Oh, so I suppose it was me! I say it was you.”
“No!”
“Yes!”
“No!”
“Yes!”
And growing angrier and angrier, they went from words to blows, and grabbing hold of each other, they scratched, bit, and knocked each other about.
When the fight was over, Master Antonio found Geppetto’s yellow wig in his hands, and Geppetto discovered the carpenter’s grey-streaked wig in his mouth.
“Give me back my wig!” shouted Master Antonio.
“And you give me back mine, and let’s make peace.”
The two little old men, after each had taken back his own wig, shook hands and swore to remain good friends for the rest of their lives.
“Well then, my friend Geppetto,” said the carpenter to show that they had made peace, “what is the favour you want from me?”
“I’d like a bit of wood to make my puppet; will you give me some?”

Master Antonio, delighted, went straight to fetch from the workbench the piece of wood that had given him so many frights. But just as he was about to hand it to his friend, the piece of wood gave a sudden jerk, and slipping violently out of his hands, struck poor Geppetto hard on his thin, dried-up shins.
“Ah! Is this your polite way of giving things away, Master Antonio? You’ve almost crippled me!…”
“I swear it wasn’t me!”
“Then I suppose it was me!…”
“It’s all this wood’s fault…”
“I know it was the wood: but you threw it at my legs!”
“I didn’t throw it at you!”
“Liar!”
“Geppetto, don’t insult me: or I’ll call you Polendina!…”
“Donkey!”
“Polendina!”
“Ass!”
“Polendina!”
“Ugly little monkey!”
“Polendina!”
Hearing himself called Polendina for the third time, Geppetto went blind with rage, threw himself at the carpenter, and they gave each other a terrible beating.

When the battle was over, Master Antonio had two more scratches on his nose, and the other man had two fewer buttons on his jacket. Having settled their scores in this way, they shook hands and swore to remain good friends for the rest of their lives.
Then Geppetto took his fine piece of wood, and after thanking Master Antonio, limped home.
